You said

I have many .wav files. I want t way to detect whether there's any speech in them.

Gemini said

You have a few good ways to tackle this, depending on whether you want a quick command-line tool, a lightweight Python script, or a heavy-duty machine learning model.

The technical term for what you're looking for is VAD (Voice Activity Detection). Here are the best ways to do it, ranked from easiest to most advanced.

Method 1: The Quick Python Way (silero-vad)

If you want something highly accurate that handles background noise well, Silero VAD is an excellent pre-trained AI model that runs locally and incredibly fast.

First, install the library:

Bash
pip install silero-vad soundfile

Then, use this quick script to check your files:

Python
import torch
import soundfile as sf

# Load the model
model, utils = torch.hub.load(repo_or_dir='snakers4/silero-vad', model='silero_vad')
(get_speech_timestamps, save_audio, read_audio, VADIterator, collect_chunks) = utils

# Load your audio file (Must be 16000Hz or 8000Hz)
audio_path = 'your_file.wav'
wav = read_audio(audio_path, sampling_rate=16000)

# Get speech timestamps
speech_timestamps = get_speech_timestamps(wav, model, sampling_rate=16000)

if speech_timestamps:
    print(f"Speech detected! Found {len(speech_timestamps)} segments of speech.")
    for segment in speech_timestamps:
        print(f"  From {segment['start']/16000:.2f}s to {segment['end']/16000:.2f}s")
else:
    print("No speech detected (just silence or noise).")

Method 2: The Lightweight Way (webrtcvad)

If you have thousands of files and need something blazing fast that doesn't use deep learning, Google's WebRTC VAD is the industry standard. It looks at the frequency and energy of the audio to detect human speech.

First, install it:

Bash
pip install webrtcvad wavio

⚠️ Note: WebRTC VAD is strict. It only accepts audio that is PCM 16-bit, sampled at 8000, 16000, 32000, or 48000 Hz, and processed in chunks of 10, 20, or 30 milliseconds.

Here is how to process a file:

Python
import webrtcvad
import wavio

def has_speech(audio_path, aggressiveness=3):
    vad = webrtcvad.Vad(aggressiveness) # 0 (lax) to 3 (strict filtering of noise)
    
    # Read wav file
    wav = wavio.read(audio_path)
    sample_rate = wav.rate
    data = wav.data
    
    # Ensure it's mono
    if len(data.shape) > 1:
        data = data[:, 0]
        
    # Convert to 16-bit bytes
    raw_audio = data.astype('int16').tobytes()
    
    # Check 30ms frames (30ms * sample_rate * 2 bytes per sample)
    frame_duration = 0.030 
    frame_size = int(sample_rate * frame_duration * 2)
    
    speech_frames = 0
    total_frames = 0
    
    for i in range(0, len(raw_audio) - frame_size, frame_size):
        frame = raw_audio[i:i+frame_size]
        total_frames += 1
        if vad.is_speech(frame, sample_rate):
            speech_frames += 1
            
    # If more than 10% of the audio contains speech, flag it
    return (speech_frames / total_frames) > 0.10

print("Contains speech:", has_speech("your_file.wav"))

Method 3: The No-Code/Command Line Way (FFmpeg)

If you just want a quick tool to run in your terminal without writing Python, you can use FFmpeg's silencedetect filter.

Run this in your terminal:

Bash
ffmpeg -i your_file.wav -af silencedetect=noise=-30dB:d=0.5 -f null -

  • noise=-30dB: Anything quieter than -30dB is considered silence (adjust this based on your noise floor).

  • d=0.5: Looks for silence periods longer than 0.5 seconds.

How to read the output: FFmpeg will spit out logs. If you see text like [silencedetect ...] silence_start and silence_end, it's finding silence. If the entire file is silence, the duration of the silence will match the duration of the file. If there are gaps in the silence, you have sound (likely speech).

Summary Recommendation

  • Choose Method 1 (Silero VAD) if your audio files have background noise (cars, static, music) because it is incredibly smart at distinguishing human voices from random sounds.

  • Choose Method 2 (WebRTC) if you have a massive volume of clean audio files and need to scan them at lightning speed.
